cultural.vision_reason: This is a large hand-woven strip-cloth man's gown (riga/tobe) with indigo "saki/etu" checked cloth and embroidered neckline panel — a style associated with Hausa/Yoruba/Mande weaving traditions of the wider West African savanna, and such gowns are worn and traded widely across the region including by Wolof men; the museum's own description even notes the Hausa/Yoruba naming, but the general form is plausible for the claimed Wolof ethnicity.

physical.title: gown; tobe
physical.summary: Man's gown (tobe, boubou, riga saki). The body is formed of 88 narrow strips, hand-woven from hand-spun indigo-dyed cotton of two shades which produce a mottled effect; the strips are hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The strips are uniform and use indigo-dyed cotton in both warp and weft, with lines of white cotton inserted frequently and regularly in both warp and weft to create a checked appearance of a blue/grey colour (known as ‘saki’ by the Hausa’ and ‘etu’ by the Yoruba). The body of the cloth is shaped by folding the strips at the top to fan out towards the bottom of the skirt, while the sleeves are wider at the top than the bottom and as a result fan out. At the front is sewn a large pocket. The pocket, shoulder and front are hand-embroidered in white cotton in a large rectangle that extends beyond the pocket . The embroidery is in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch, and in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The knives themselves are embroidered on top of extra pieces of cloth that have been cut to shape. The edge along the bottom of the gown has been lined with a wide patch of strip-woven cotton which uses magenta 'alaari' silk with lines of white cotton running through it at an oblique angle; this has been attached to the gown by sewing in white thread that can be seen from the front.
